source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases
finding: The founding paper names three heuristics: representativeness, availability, and anchoring and adjustment. They are cheap and usually work, but cause systematic, predictable errors. Method: compare intuition to probability rules, then look for the heuristic behind each error.
numbers: Science 185(4157):1124-1131. Biases are listed in sections under the three heuristics.
quote: highly economical and usually effective, but they also produce predictable biases
limits: Short vignette studies, many cited from other work, sample sizes mostly not given. No process model: heuristics are named, not formalised.
agent_relevance: S1 input hygiene: a model reading a prompt meets the same three cue types (similarity, ease of recall, a number already in view). Use them as a checklist of input contamination.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) - base rate (engineer/lawyer) section
finding: Representativeness: people ignore prior probabilities when a personality sketch is given, even a worthless one. With no sketch they use the base rate correctly; with a worthless sketch they say .5.
numbers: Base rates .7 vs .3 engineers. No sketch: judged .7 and .3. Worthless sketch of 'Dick': judged .5 in both base-rate conditions.
quote: when worthless evidence is given, prior probabilities are ignored
limits: Sample sizes not given in the 1974 article (they come from Kahneman & Tversky 1973). Effect shrinks when the sketch is clearly random.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant but vivid detail can erase a correct prior. A scaffold should state priors first and strip descriptive filler before judging.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) - sample size (hospital problem)
finding: Insensitivity to sample size: most people think a large and a small hospital are equally likely to record days with more than 60 percent boys. The smaller hospital is the right answer.
numbers: Large hospital 45 births a day, small 15. Choices: larger 21, smaller 21, about the same 53 (about 95 subjects, counts as printed).
limits: Counts only, no test. The same weak small-sample sense is found in experienced researchers (law of small numbers).
agent_relevance: Binz & Schulz found GPT-3 also says 'about equal'. A check that asks how big the sample is before judging may help.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) - misconceptions of chance
finding: People expect a short random sequence to look random: H-T-H-T-T-H is judged more likely than H-H-H-T-T-T. They hold the gambler's fallacy. Chance is seen as self-correcting; in fact deviations are diluted, not corrected.
numbers: Qualitative examples; no counts in this article.
limits: Cited work, not new data. Holds for experienced psychologists too.
agent_relevance: Do not read local patterns in a few samples from one model as signal (matches guardrail G4).

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) - availability: words, committees, imaginability
finding: Availability: frequency is judged by how easily instances come to mind. People say more words start with r or k than have it third, though the reverse is true. Small committees seem more numerous than large ones.
numbers: Committees from 10 people: median estimate 70 for 2-member and 20 for 8-member committees; correct answer 45 for both. Abstract words judged much more frequent than concrete words of equal frequency.
limits: Ease of retrieval vs number of instances is not separated here (Schwarz et al. split them later). The r/k result also fits a search-structure account.
agent_relevance: LLM analog: what is easy to generate is what was common in training text. Ask for base counts, not impressions.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) - anchoring and adjustment (wheel of fortune)
finding: A random number from a wheel of fortune moved estimates of the percent of African countries in the UN. Payoffs for accuracy did not remove the effect.
numbers: Median estimate 25 for anchor 10 and 45 for anchor 65 (group N not given in this article).
quote: Payoffs for accuracy did not reduce the anchoring effect.
limits: N not stated. Later critics say subjects may read the number as informative. Self-generated anchors work differently (Epley & Gilovich).
agent_relevance: Only a number in view is needed. Do not put a candidate answer, a prior attempt or an expert guess in the prompt before the independent estimate is made.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) - anchoring by incomplete computation
finding: Anchoring also arises from the subject's own partial computation. High school students had 5 seconds to estimate 8x7x6x5x4x3x2x1 or the reverse order. Both groups underestimated; the descending order gave higher estimates.
numbers: Median 512 (ascending) vs 2,250 (descending). Correct answer 40,320.
limits: Medians only, N not given. Shows insufficient adjustment but does not test the mechanism.
agent_relevance: A model that writes a quick answer after a few steps sets its own anchor for later steps. Supports checking final answers with code instead of extending a first guess (G2).

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) - conjunctive/disjunctive events and confidence intervals
finding: Anchoring on the probability of one step makes people overrate conjunctions (long plans) and underrate disjunctions. Confidence intervals are too narrow because the best estimate anchors both bounds, and calibration depends on how the interval is elicited.
numbers: Bar-Hillel bets: conjunctive event (.48) preferred to simple (.50); simple preferred to disjunctive (.52). Intervals: true value outside the 98 percent-type interval for about 30 percent of problems. 24 quantities: group 1 events judged p=.10 occurred 24 percent; group 2 (given median as start) judged mean .34, actual 26 percent; median odds stated 3:1 instead of 9:1.
limits: Calibration depends on elicitation procedure, so part of the overconfidence is procedure-driven.
agent_relevance: Plan success estimates built by chaining steps will be overstated. Use external base rates for task success.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983 citation-classic note on the 1974 paper)
finding: Authors' own account: research began in 1969, took years and thousands of subject hours, and the paper was written over 1973. The approach: compare intuition to normative principles, search for heuristics behind errors, and study the biases they cause.
numbers: Over 420 citations by 1983 (per the note).
limits: Author self-report; hindsight narrative.
agent_relevance: Shows the programme is descriptive and heuristic-first, not a formal model.

source: Wikipedia: Anchoring effect (accessed 2026-11-01; secondary)
finding: Three accounts: (1) anchoring-and-adjustment, insufficient adjustment (T&K); (2) selective accessibility, a form of semantic priming (Strack & Mussweiler); (3) attitude change. Self-generated anchors: people stop adjusting at the edge of a plausible range (Epley & Gilovich). Warning people did not remove anchoring; consider-the-opposite is the most reliable debiaser; money incentives had mixed effects.
numbers: Gandhi death age with anchors 9 vs 140: mean guesses 50 vs 67. Ariely social-security-number bids 60 to 120 percent higher in the high-number group. Studies with clearly random anchors (die roll, random button) failed to replicate the effect.
limits: Secondary source; check against cited papers. Cause of anchoring is unresolved.
agent_relevance: Design rule: remove anchors from the prompt rather than ask the model to ignore them. Lou & Sun find the ignore instruction fails in GPT-4.

source: Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995), as reported in a LessWrong replication review
finding: Original study: 15 quantities, 156 Berkeley students; a greater/less question with a high or low anchor shifted later estimates a lot.
numbers: N=156 students, 15 quantities. Mississippi length median 800 miles with no anchor, 300 with a 70-mile anchor, 1,500 with a 2,000-mile anchor.
limits: Blog post: numbers are the blogger's reading of the paper and OSF data, not a primary report.
agent_relevance: One comparison question against a number is enough to shift the estimate that follows.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Many Labs 1 anchoring items, as tabulated in the same LessWrong review
finding: Anchoring replicated on all four items. Raw gaps between low- and high-anchor estimates were smaller than the original, but the standardised effect size was reported larger because the design changed to between-subjects.
numbers: Babies born per day (US): original 1k vs 40k; replication 3.2k vs 26.7k. Chicago: 600k vs 5.05m; replication 1.03m vs 3.00m. Everest: 8k vs 42.55k; replication 11.8k vs 34.5k. SF-NYC: 2.6k vs 4k; replication 2.85k vs 3.99k miles. About 5,000 participants.
limits: Secondary tabulation; I did not open Klein et al. itself. Design differences (told the anchor, not a comparison question for Chicago).
agent_relevance: Numeric anchoring is among the most robust effects in the field, so it is the first bias to hygiene-proof.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2 - overall and incidental anchors
finding: Preregistered replication of 28 findings in 125 samples (15,305 participants, 36 countries). 15 of 28 (54 percent) replicated at p<.05. Median effect size fell from d=0.60 in originals to d=0.15. Incidental anchors did not replicate.
numbers: Incidental anchor (phone named P97 vs P17; Critcher & Gilovich 2008): original d=0.30, N=207; replication d=0.04, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.09], N=6,826, not significant. 9 of 28 effects went in the opposite direction.
limits: This anchor is incidental and weak, not the classic numeric comparison.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: anchors unrelated to the task may do little. Anchors that enter the task as a plausible answer are the risk.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2 - framing item (discounted item, from T&K 1981 Study 10)
finding: A framing item from T&K 1981 (cost of a discounted item, jacket-and-calculator type) replicated at under half the original size.
numbers: Original: 68 percent vs 29 percent would travel, OR=4.96, N=181. Replication N=7,228: 49 percent vs 32 percent, OR=2.06, 95% CI [1.87, 2.27], d=0.40.
limits: This is the relative-saving item, not the Asian disease problem. I did not find the Asian disease problem in Many Labs 2.
agent_relevance: Framing survives large-scale replication but shrinks. Do not use the original magnitude as a prior.

source: Wikipedia: Framing effect (psychology) (accessed 2026-11-01; secondary)
finding: Asian disease problem (T&K 1981): equal outcomes get opposite choices depending on whether they are worded as lives saved or lives lost. Two variables: framing (positive vs negative) and certainty (certain vs risky).
numbers: 72 percent chose the sure option when worded as 'saves 200 lives'; 78 percent chose the risky option when worded as deaths.
limits: Secondary; N not given here; replication spread across wordings not checked.
agent_relevance: Pairs of equivalent prompts worded as gain or loss are a cheap test for framing sensitivity and a consistency check.

source: Wikipedia: Conjunction fallacy (accessed 2026-11-01; secondary)
finding: Linda problem: most chose 'bank teller and feminist' over 'bank teller'. Gigerenzer and Hertwig said the wording is ambiguous ('probable', 'and'). A frequency format ('out of 100 people, how many') cuts the error sharply, as do set-relation and Venn-diagram cues. Some frequency-only tasks still produce the fallacy.
numbers: About 85 percent gave the conjunction answer in the original; with the wording 'whether or not feminist' 57 percent still did; with frequency format about 20 percent.
limits: Secondary; the 85 and 20 percent figures come from T&K 1983 and later work, not checked in the originals.
agent_relevance: Recasting a probability question as counts of cases is a known repair and fits the schema's restate-the-problem operator.

source: Wikipedia: Representativeness heuristic (accessed 2026-11-01; secondary)
finding: Tom W. study (K&T 1973): likelihood judgements track similarity ratings, not base rates. Cab problem: people give over 50 percent, often 80, while Bayes gives 41 percent.
numbers: Over 95 percent said Tom more likely studies computer science than education or humanities despite larger base rates there. Cab: 85 percent Green, 15 percent Blue, witness 80 percent reliable gives 41 percent (0.12 / 0.29).
limits: Secondary. Cab effect shrinks when the base rate is made causal (not shown here).
agent_relevance: Binz & Schulz report GPT-3 does not fall for the cab problem. A Bayes check in code removes the bias.

source: Wikipedia: Availability heuristic (accessed 2026-11-01; secondary)
finding: Availability splits into number of instances recalled vs ease of retrieval (Schwarz et al.). People rated themselves less assertive after recalling 12 examples than 6, because 12 was harder. Famous-name lists: the gender with more famous names was judged more frequent.
numbers: Lists of 19 famous women and 20 less famous men (and the reverse): famous names were recalled more and most judged that gender more frequent. Schwarz: recall of 6 vs 12 assertive behaviours.
limits: Secondary. Critics say the ease-of-retrieval account has mixed support and that K-word results may reflect how words are stored.
agent_relevance: Do not infer frequency from how many items the model can write. Asking for more examples may lower confidence, as in humans (untested idea).

source: Wikipedia: Heuristic (psychology) (accessed 2026-11-01; secondary)
finding: Attribute substitution: a hard question is replaced by an easier related one without awareness. Rival views: heuristics as laziness, as natural assessments, or as ecologically tuned tools (Gigerenzer). High CRT scorers commit the conjunction fallacy less.
numbers: 98 percent confidence intervals are wrong 30 to 40 percent of the time in much-replicated work.
limits: Secondary. The K&T model is verbal and makes no ex ante quantitative predictions, which is Gigerenzer's main objection.
agent_relevance: Attribute substitution matches an LLM answering a nearby, easier question. A restate-and-check step in S1 can test that the question answered is the question asked.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 fell for the Linda conjunction fallacy and the small-hospital item, but not the cab base-rate item. On CRT it gave the intuitive wrong answer on all three items. It showed framing, certainty and overweighting effects (3 of 6 prospect-theory effects).
numbers: Linda: chose the conjunction. Cab: roughly correct. Hospital: 'about equal'. CRT 1-3: intuitive, wrong. 13,000+ gamble problems: only Davinci above chance, below humans (t(29134)=-11.50).
limits: One model (GPT-3 family, 2022), single vignettes, no sample statistics for vignettes.
agent_relevance: Biases in LLMs are item-specific. Test each one; assume none.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee & Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? (GPT-3.5)
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) showed anchoring, the conjunction fallacy, framing and the endowment effect, with mTurk humans as comparison. Anchoring: a self-chosen number in a low (10-20) or high (100-200) range shifted a later estimate of books in a bartender's house.
numbers: Anchoring: low anchor mean 20.83 (SE 3.38) ChatGPT vs 22.50 (3.57) humans; high anchor 105.97 (SE 9.08) vs 80.50 (9.81); ChatGPT t(58)=8.78, humans t(58)=5.55, both p<.0001; n=30 per cell. Framing: ChatGPT rated a drug 5 (positive) vs 4 (negative) in all 11 trials each; humans 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, N=82. Conjunction: ChatGPT chose it 18 of 20; humans 10 of 20. GPT-4, 5 trials per cell: anchor means 22.0 vs 94.33.
quote: language may play a role in generating these effects in humans
limits: Small N. Money prompts avoided because the model refused. Anchor was model-generated. Prompts were not the originals.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a number in context moves an LLM estimate as much as it moves humans. Keep anchors out of the prompt before the independent estimate.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of LLMs via human cognitive biases
finding: Code models (Codex, CodeGen) show framing- and anchoring-like failures: irrelevant preceding code cuts accuracy and the framing line is copied; an anchor function with an error cuts accuracy and its lines leak into outputs.
numbers: HumanEval baseline accuracy 32.9 percent (Codex), 25.6 percent (CodeGen). With an irrelevant preceding function and 'raise NotImplemented': accuracy 2.4 and 1.5 percent; the framing line was output 91.7 and 79.3 percent of the time. Print-var anchor: 'for var in' in 32 to 61 percent of Codex solutions; print(var) in 26 to 44 percent.
limits: Code models of 2021-22, not chat models. 'Framing' here is closer to prompt contamination than gain/loss framing.
agent_relevance: Strong support for S1 hygiene: irrelevant or wrong material placed before the task leaks into the answer. Keep failed attempts out of fresh attempts' prompts.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: 13,465 admissions prompts. GPT-4 showed a strong framing effect; models showed primacy (options A, B chosen over C, D). Few-shot mitigation caused failures; the self-help method (the model rewrites its own prompt to remove bias) worked best.
numbers: Framing (admit vs reject wording), difference in admission rate: GPT-4 -0.405 baseline (40.5 percent more admitted under reject framing), GPT-3.5 +0.165; after self-help GPT-4 -0.010. Counterfactual few-shot raised GPT-4 gap to -0.570. Anchoring decision-confidence distance d: GPT-4 baseline 0.317.
limits: One task (admissions); anchoring is proxied by order effects; some results near 0 or 1 reflect broken instruction following, not lack of bias.
agent_relevance: Examples in the prompt can add new biases or break instruction following. Self-rewrite of the prompt is a candidate S1 operator.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study
finding: 62 questions, each with a neutral fact hint plus a low or high anchor. GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and GPT-4o were pulled toward anchors; stronger models more consistently; expert-opinion anchors the strongest. Chain of thought, thoughts of principles, 'ignore the hint' and reflection did not reduce it. Giving both a low and a high hint helped when they bracketed the truth.
numbers: 62 questions, 3 hints each. 12 expert-anchor questions had no exceptions. Time-period questions: 7 of 42 questions but 6 of 11 non-significant exceptions; 9 of the 11 exceptions came from GPT-3.5.
limits: Small dataset, per-question t-tests, preprint by school students; treat with care.
agent_relevance: Tests the common mitigations for numeric anchors: they fail. Remove the anchor from the prompt, or present opposing anchors, instead of asking the model to ignore it.

source: Shaki, Kraus & Wooldridge (2023) Cognitive effects in large language models
finding: GPT-3 showed priming, distance, SNARC and size-congruity effects but no anchoring. The anchoring task used code-completion estimates of sequence length, chosen so the model could not know the answer.
numbers: 4 experiments, 838 items, 21 analysed lengths. Mean estimate small-anchor vs large-anchor: 41.5 vs 41.28 (p=.51); 41.08 vs 39.90 (p=.006); 45.78 vs 42.04 (p<.001); 48.86 vs 46.31 (p<.001). In the last two the effect is reversed.
limits: GPT-3 base model with an unusual code-style prompt. Contrast with Suri (chat model, natural-language anchor): task format decides whether anchoring shows.
agent_relevance: A failed-anchoring result. Test on the agent's own prompt format; do not assume either way.

source: Itzhak et al. (2024) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned LMs show emergent cognitive bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decoy, certainty and belief biases in GPT-3, T5 and Mistral families. Bias score = share choosing the target in treatment minus share in control.
numbers: Bias scores range from -1 to 1. Tuned models mostly higher, e.g. certainty effect up to 0.67 (text-davinci-003) and belief-invalid up to 0.65; some base models near 0 (e.g. 0.00 belief-valid for DaVinci).
limits: Table layout in the PDF text is hard to read, so the model-to-number mapping is approximate. Decoy and belief are not the three core heuristics.
agent_relevance: Alignment training can add human-like biases. A better chat model may be more exposed to input framing, not less.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: Seven LLMs on classic K&T tasks (Linda, hospital, base rate and others). Models are irrational but mostly not in the human way: most wrong answers were illogical rather than the human bias, and answers to one prompt were inconsistent.
numbers: Correct with correct reasoning: GPT-4 69.2 percent, Claude 2 55.0, Bard 35.8, GPT-3.5 29.2, Llama 2-70b 15.0, 13b 5.0, 7b 2.5 percent. Human-like biased answers: GPT-3.5 21.7 percent (50.8 including human-like correct). Llama 2-70b refused 41.7 percent. Total human-like: GPT-4 73.3 percent, Llama 2-13b 8.3 percent.
limits: Default parameters, no system prompt, about 12 tasks with repeats, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: The errors are not always human errors, so human debiasing lore may not transfer. Inconsistent answers support counted agreement and code checks (G4).

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Early GPT-3 models answer CRT and semantic-illusion tasks intuitively; ChatGPT and GPT-4 do not. The shift comes with chain-of-thought text. Forcing chain of thought on davinci-003, or blocking it in ChatGPT, moves accuracy back.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks: davinci-003 5 percent correct, 80 percent intuitive; ChatGPT-3.5 59 percent correct, 15 percent intuitive; ChatGPT-4 96 percent correct, 0 percent intuitive; 500 humans 38 percent correct, 55 percent intuitive. Chain of thought on davinci-003: correct 5 to 28 percent, intuitive 80 to 29 percent.
limits: CRT is a reflection test, not one of the three core heuristics. CRT items are public and may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Bias in LLMs is not fixed: written reasoning before the answer can move output from System 1-like to System 2-like. But Lou & Sun found chain of thought did not fix numeric anchoring.

source: Formal-model status of the heuristics-and-biases programme (from Wikipedia: Heuristic (psychology) and Anchoring effect)
finding: No formal computational model of the three heuristics: they are verbal. Later partial models: selective accessibility and attitude-change accounts of anchoring; Epley & Gilovich's plausible-range stopping rule for self-generated anchors; Gigerenzer's demand for formal models that predict ex ante.
numbers: No quantitative fit statistics collected.
limits: Based on secondary descriptions; I did not open Epley & Gilovich (2001, 2006), Strack & Mussweiler (1997) or Gigerenzer (1996).
agent_relevance: The agent can use 'adjust from an anchor' as a model of its own behaviour only if tested; otherwise treat as unmodelled.
